pageInfo.subtitle: Transform aimless scale running into intentional, melodic guitar solos that outline the harmony section by section.
pageInfo.heroDescription: The secret separating amateur scale-running from authoritative, melodic guitar solos is knowing which notes matter most over each changing chord. Chord tone soloing teaches you to target the Root, 3rd, 5th, and 7th of every chord right as the harmony shifts. Instead of hoping a generic scale pattern happens to sound good, you will outline chord changes with crystalline clarity, connecting chord tones with passing notes, enclosures, and smooth voice leading like Larry Carlton, Robben Ford, and David Gilmour.

items.text: The Root (Tonic Anchor): The most stable, resting pitch. Great for phrase endings and establishing home base, but overusing it makes solos sound predictable.
The 3rd (The Color Note): The single most important note for a soloist. It defines whether the chord is Major or Minor and injects immediate sweetness or sorrow.
The 5th (The Consonant Pillar): Provides powerful harmonic stability without emotional tension, serving as an ideal staging ground for melodic leaps.
The 7th (The Guide Tone): Creates magnetic pull toward the next chord. In dominant and jazz chords, the 7th resolves down by half-step to the 3rd of the following chord.
Scale Passing Tones: Notes 2, 4, and 6 act as melodic bridges connecting the strong chord tones together.
Strong Beats for Strong Notes: Land on chord tones (especially the 3rd or Root) squarely on beats 1 and 3 to ground the listener's ear.
Chord Shape Visualization: Visualize the underlying barre or open chord grip beneath your scale patterns at all times.
Anticipate the Change: Target notes can be hit a half-beat or eighth-note early to create compelling melodic anticipation.
Chromatic Enclosures: Surround your target chord tone by playing one fret above, one fret below, and resolving onto the target note.
Guide-Tone Paths: Connect progressions by tracking how 3rds and 7ths move smoothly by step from measure to measure.

exercises.title: Root Note Targeting over I-vi-IV-V (The Anchor)
exercises.description: The first step in chord tone soloing is mental geography: knowing exactly where the root of the active chord sits on your fretboard before it arrives. In this 4-bar study over C - Am - F - G, you play simple melodic lines from the C major scale, but you must land decisively on the ROOT of each chord on beat 1 (C, A, F, and G).

patternNote.text: Rule: Land on Root C (fret 8, string 6) ➔ Root A (fret 5, string 6) ➔ Root F (fret 1, string 6) ➔ Root G (fret 3, string 6) on beat 1

notation.title: Root Note Targeting over C - Am - F - G
notation.staveTitle: Landing on the Root of Each Chord on Beat 1

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Set your metronome to 75 BPM. Speak the chord names out loud one beat before they change. Notice how striking the root on beat 1 gives your phrase instant grounding and certainty.

exercises.title: The Defining 3rd (Major vs Minor Color)
exercises.description: Targeting the 3rd is the single most transformative breakthrough for any improviser. While the root provides stability, the 3rd defines the chord's emotional DNA. Over C major you target E (major 3rd); over A minor you target C (minor 3rd); over F major you target A; over G major you target B. Listen to how your solo instantly 'sings' the underlying chords.

patternNote.text: Target Notes: E (3rd of C) ➔ C (b3 of Am) ➔ A (3rd of F) ➔ B (3rd of G)

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Compare Exercise 1 and Exercise 2 back to back. Notice how targeting the 3rd sounds far more mature, expressive, and melodic than landing on the root.

exercises.title: 7th and 5th Color Accents over ii-V-I
exercises.description: In jazz, R&B, and sophisticated pop, 7th chords rule the harmony. Over a standard Dm7 - G7 - Cmaj7 progression, targeting the 7th of the chord introduces sophisticated tension. In this exercise, you target C (the minor 7th of Dm7), F (the dominant 7th of G7), and B (the major 7th of Cmaj7) before resolving gracefully onto the root.

patternNote.text: Progression: Dm7 (target C, b7) ➔ G7 (target F, b7) ➔ Cmaj7 (target B, 7) resolving to C

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Notice how the 7th of G7 (F) pulls with intense harmonic magnetism toward the 3rd of Cmaj7 (E). This voice-leading step is the engine of western harmony.

exercises.title: Guide Tone Voice Leading (7th Resolving to 3rd)
exercises.description: Guide tones are the 3rds and 7ths of chords that define the harmonic progression. In a ii-V-I sequence, the 7th of the ii chord (C in Dm7) resolves down a half-step to become the 3rd of the V chord (B in G7). Then, the 7th of the V chord (F in G7) resolves down a half-step to become the 3rd of the I chord (E in Cmaj7). Mastering this line guarantees seamless transitions across any jazz or pop standard.

patternNote.text: Voice Leading Thread: C (b7 of Dm7) ➔ B (3rd of G7) ➔ F (b7 of G7) ➔ E (3rd of Cmaj7)

notation.title: Guide Tone Voice Leading in ii-V-I
notation.staveTitle: Stepwise Guide Tone Descent Across Changes

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Play this exercise with a smooth legato feel. Notice how you do not need to play dozens of notes to outline the chords—the guide tone motion does all the harmonic heavy lifting.

exercises.title: Chromatic Enclosures Around Target 3rds
exercises.description: An enclosure is a bebop and modern blues technique where you surround a target chord tone before landing on it. To enclose the 3rd of C (E note at fret 7, string 5), you play one half-step above (F), one half-step below (D#), and then land squarely on E on beat 1. This generates sophisticated tension and release that sounds instantly professional.

patternNote.text: Enclosure Formula: Half-step above ➔ Half-step below ➔ TARGET CHORD TONE

notation.title: Chromatic Enclosure Etude
notation.staveTitle: Surrounding 3rds with Upper and Lower Neighbors

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: The magic of enclosures is rhythmic placement: the chromatic outside notes must occur on the weak eighth notes, resolving onto the target chord tone on the downbeat.

exercises.title: Connecting Arpeggios with Diatonic Passing Tones
exercises.description: Playing pure arpeggios can sound mechanical, while playing pure scales can sound unfocused. The solution is weaving scale passing tones between arpeggio chord tones. This study outlines C, Am, and F arpeggios while using smooth scale steps to connect between the chord tones.

patternNote.text: Concept: Arpeggio framework (1-3-5) bridged by diatonic passing tones (2, 4, 6)

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Use continuous alternate picking across the 6th, 5th, 4th, and 3rd strings. Keep your fret-hand fingers close to the strings to maintain smooth transitions.

exercises.title: The Master Solo Etude (Complete Harmonic Performance)
exercises.description: Put everything together in this expressive 4-bar performance study over C - Am - F - G. Notice how each measure opens with a target 3rd, incorporates expressive vocal vibrato, and uses passing tones to navigate seamlessly to the next chord change.

patternNote.text: Full Application: Target 3rd on Beat 1 ➔ Melodic Passing Line ➔ Smooth Voice Leading

notation.title: Chord Tone Performance Solo over C - Am - F - G
notation.staveTitle: Complete Musical Solo Outlining the Harmony

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Record yourself playing this solo over a slow C - Am - F - G backing track. Listen back with your eyes closed: can you clearly identify the chord changes purely from your lead guitar notes?

tips.title: Critical Pitfalls, Pro Insights & Practice Routines

items.title: 3 Mistakes That Kill Chord Tone Soloing
items: The Root Rut: Landing exclusively on root notes, making your solos sound like the bassline rather than an expressive melodic voice.
Ignoring the Defining 3rd: Playing minor pentatonic runs over major chords without resolving to the major 3rd, causing harsh clashing dissonance.
Mechanical Arpeggio Raking: Playing pure textbook arpeggios up and down without musical pauses or passing tones, sounding like finger exercises instead of music.

items.title: Masters of Chord Tone Soloing
items: Larry Carlton ('Kid Charlemagne'): The undisputed benchmark of targeting 3rds and 7ths through complex Steely Dan changes with sweet vocal sustain.
Robben Ford ('Talk to Your Daughter'): Flawlessly merges minor blues grit with sophisticated major-3rd target resolutions.
David Gilmour ('Comfortably Numb'): Soaring slow-blues bends that land squarely on active chord tones on strong beats with maximum emotional release.
George Benson ('Breezin''): Effortless bebop enclosures and arpeggiated lines outlining jazz-funk progressions with immaculate timing.

items.title: The 15-Minute Daily Chord Tone Workout
items: Phase 1: 3rd Targeting Isolation (5 min) - Put on a 2-chord vamp (e.g. C to F). Play only the 3rd of each chord (E on C, A on F) on beat 1 with wide vibrato.
Phase 2: Two-Note Approach Lines (5 min) - Lead into each target 3rd using two diatonic scale steps from above or below.
Phase 3: Chromatic Enclosure Workout (5 min) - Practice surrounding target 3rds with upper and lower half-step chromatic neighbors before landing on beat 1.
